h1:
Pak Chong Night Markets
Eat All Night, Easy on the Wallet
intro: After a full day of hiking the national park and hopping cafes, evenings are when Khao Yai locals and visitors head to the night markets in downtown Pak Chong. You can graze your way from grilled skewers and fried snacks to cold desserts, with prices starting in the double digits. Some stalls have been running so long they have a regular queue. This is your guide to which markets to visit, what days they open, and the dishes people keep talking about.
chips: 🦪 Fried oyster omelette & fish maw soup

blocks.html: Pak Chong is the gateway to Khao Yai. The town sits along the Mittraphap Highway, about 20–25 km from the Pak Chong-side park entrance. Once the sun goes down it turns into a grazing district by default, with several night markets spread around town — some open daily, some only on weekends. We've picked out the ones that are genuinely still running and packed with food, with ballpark prices based on real reviews (prices move up and down with ingredients and the festival season).

blocks.text: The main night markets in Pak Chong–Khao Yai

items.name: Pak Chong Night Market (Night Bazaar)
items.blurb: The town's main night market, near the old Mittraphap Highway by the Pak Chong fresh market. Food stalls line both sides of the street. Open daily from around 17:00, with roadside parking.

items.name: Pak Chong Khlong Thom Market
items.blurb: A bigger market with 200-plus stalls — food, secondhand goods, clothing, and kids' rides. Good for families, and easier to wander than the other spots.

items.name: Teen Khao Night Market, Khao Yai
items.blurb: The chilled-out night market, with live music on some nights, food and drinks, and a relaxed sit-and-hang vibe at the foot of the hills. Check the market's page before you go — opening days aren't fixed.

blocks.title: Plan before you go
blocks.html: Pak Chong Night Market is open daily, so it's your safest bet on a weeknight. The more laid-back spots like Teen Khao tend to be liveliest Friday–Saturday. If you're set on one particular stall, check the market's Facebook page for that day before heading out.

blocks.html: The food at Pak Chong's night markets is no-fuss street food — easy to eat, friendly on the wallet. We've ordered these by how often the names come up in reviews and food-crawl clips. Prices are estimated ranges, and some items sell out fast if you turn up late.

items.name: Fried oyster omelette (or-suan), Night Market
items.blurb: The signature stall of Pak Chong Night Market — crispy batter, soft egg, plump oysters. It's the dish reviewers mention most at this market, and you may have to wait in line when it's busy.

items.name: Fish maw soup, Tong Tong
items.blurb: Thick fish maw soup loaded with toppings — another stall that often draws a queue until the pot runs dry. Best eaten warm in the evening, especially on a cool night.

items.name: Grilled pork, chicken & skewers
items.blurb: The heart of every night market — grilled fresh, the fragrant smoke trailing the whole way down the street. Grilled pork, chicken, wings, grilled intestines: snack on them as you walk or grab some to take back to your room.

items.name: Dim sum & steamed buns, Night zone
items.blurb: There are dim sum stalls in the night-market zone on the Mittraphap Highway side, starting around ฿35 per basket — har gow, dumplings, steamed buns. Order a few kinds to share.

items.name: Mango sticky rice, Mae Khamporn
items.blurb: Soft coconut sticky rice with sweet ripe mango — the market's go-to dessert, and one plenty of reviewers rate highly. Great to finish a meal or take home.

items.name: Som tam, grilled chicken & larb
items.blurb: You're in Isan country, so there has to be a som tam stall. Pounded fresh, spice to order, eaten with grilled chicken and sticky rice — a proper, filling meal for a couple of hundred baht.

items.name: Fried meatballs & grilled Isan sausage
items.blurb: Popular grab-and-go snacks — grilled and fried meatballs, tangy Isan sausage on skewers, with a punchy dipping sauce to add yourself.

items.name: Roti, khanom buang & honeycomb cake
items.blurb: The dough-and-sweets corner — banana roti with condensed milk, sweet-and-savoury khanom buang, hot honeycomb cake fresh off the griddle. A good last bite before you head off.

items.name: Fruit smoothies, milk tea & cold drinks
items.blurb: After a run of spicy, fried things you'll need something to cool down. Fruit smoothies, bubble milk tea, herbal drinks — a few baht a cup, easy to carry as you walk.

items.name: Local souvenirs & seasonal fruit
items.blurb: Pak Chong is fruit country, and the markets have custard apple, jackfruit, grapes and seasonal fruit at orchard-direct prices, plus sausage and mu yo to take home.

blocks.title: Eat well and don't miss the good stuff
blocks.html: The famous stalls like the oyster omelette and fish maw soup tend to draw queues and sell out fast on weekend nights. If you want to be sure, go early evening, 18:00–19:00 — you'll get it fresh without a long wait. Bring cash too, since many stalls still don't take transfers or cards.

blocks.text: How to eat your way through (a 2-night plan)

blocks.html: If you're staying in Khao Yai for 2 nights, split the two markets across two evenings — you'll get different vibes and won't get bored. Here's an easy idea for pacing your way through.

blocks.label: Night 1
blocks.title: Pak Chong Night Market — full-on food crawl

items.activity: Arrive early evening and start with grilled skewers to snack on while you scope out the market.
Head straight to the oyster omelette and Tong Tong fish maw soup before the crowds, and order to share.
items.note: These two sell out fast on weekends

items.activity: Follow up with som tam, grilled chicken and sticky rice for a proper, filling meal.
Finish with mango sticky rice or roti, then grab some fruit to take back to your room.
items.note: Bring cash — many stalls don't take transfers

blocks.label: Night 2
blocks.title: Khlong Thom / Teen Khao — a relaxed wander

items.activity: Head to Khlong Thom market, walk the food zone first, then loop the secondhand and clothing sections.
items.note: Big market — leave extra time for walking

items.activity: If it's Friday–Saturday, swing by Teen Khao Night Market for some easy live music.
items.note: Check the market's page for that day — opening days aren't fixed

items.activity: Grab snacks — fried meatballs, Isan sausage — with a cold drink and settle in.
Pick up local souvenirs — custard apple, grapes, mu yo — to take home.
items.note: Pak Chong fruit is fresh and well priced

blocks.text: Getting there and what to know

items: Take care driving down from the park in the evening — Khao Yai's roads are winding and dark, and wildlife can cross at any point. Drive slowly, keep your lights on, and don't rush down to the market.
Long-weekend nights mean traffic and rooms fill fast — if you're coming during a festival or long weekend, book your stay ahead and allow extra time to get into downtown Pak Chong.
Bring cash — most street-food stalls take cash; some have a QR code, but not all of them.
Parking — Pak Chong Night Market has roadside parking, while the bigger markets usually have a lot, though on weekend nights you may have to park further out and walk in.
Go early rather than late — the best stalls sell out fast, and some start packing up before midnight.

faq.q: What days and hours are the Pak Chong night markets open?
faq.a: Pak Chong Night Market (Night Bazaar) is open daily from around 17:00 — your safest bet on a weeknight. The more laid-back spots like Teen Khao Night Market have unfixed opening days and are liveliest Friday–Saturday, so check the market's Facebook page before you go.

faq.q: What are the must-try dishes at Pak Chong Night Market?
faq.a: The ones reviewers mention most are the fried oyster omelette and the Tong Tong fish maw soup, which often have queues and sell out fast, plus the Mae Khamporn mango sticky rice, and the grilled skewers, dim sum and som tam with grilled chicken you'll find all over the market.

faq.q: Roughly how much does the food cost?
faq.a: These are friendly street-food prices. Grilled skewers start at ฿10–25 each, plated dishes like the oyster omelette or som tam with grilled chicken run around ฿40–100, and desserts and drinks are ฿20–50. You can eat well for a few hundred baht per person (prices shift with the time of year).

faq.q: Are the markets far from Khao Yai National Park?
faq.a: The markets are in downtown Pak Chong, about 20–25 km from the Pak Chong-side park entrance. Drive carefully coming down in the evening — the road is winding and wildlife crosses it — so go slow and keep your lights on.

faq.q: Can I bring kids or the family?
faq.a: Yes. Pak Chong Khlong Thom Market is especially good for families, with wide walking space, a varied food zone, and kids' rides — easier to stroll than the roadside markets.
